answers.headline: No. Injuring someone is a crime in Spain, and even hitting someone without injuring them is punished with a fine.
answers.summary: Causing an injury that needs medical treatment is the crime of lesiones. Minor injuries and hitting someone without causing injury are punished with fines, but only if the victim files a complaint.
answers.penalties: Injury needing treatment: 3 months to 3 years in prison or a fine. Minor injury: a fine of 1–3 months. Hitting without injury: a fine of 1–2 months.

answers.headline: No. Offering an official, including a police officer, a gift or payment is a crime in Spain.
answers.summary: Offering or giving any kind of gift or payment to an authority or public official, so they act against their duties, do or delay their job, or simply because of their position, is bribery (cohecho). The person paying gets the same prison and fine as the official.
answers.penalties: The same prison term and fine as the bribed official.

answers.headline: No. Buying goods you know were stolen is a crime in Spain.
answers.summary: Receiving, buying or hiding goods for gain, knowing they come from a crime against property, is handling stolen goods (receptación). The penalty is higher for items of cultural value, essential goods, or infrastructure such as cables.
answers.penalties: 6 months to 2 years in prison; 1 to 3 years in aggravated cases.

answers.headline: No. It’s banned to drive wearing headphones, earphones or an audio headset.
answers.summary: Driving with any audio headset, earphones or similar device connected to a sound player or receiver is banned. The only exception is certified intercom or navigation systems built into motorcycle and moped helmets.
answers.penalties: A traffic fine and points off your licence.

answers.headline: No. The limit is 0.5 g/l of blood, or 0.3 g/l in your first two years and for professional drivers.
answers.summary: The limit is 0.5 g/l in blood (0.25 mg/l in breath) for drivers, including cyclists. It’s 0.3 g/l (0.15 mg/l in breath) for the first two years after getting your licence, and for drivers of trucks, buses, taxis, school transport and emergency vehicles. Above 1.2 g/l (0.60 mg/l in breath), or when under the influence, it’s a crime.
conditions: General limit: 0.5 g/l blood (0.25 mg/l breath), cyclists included
New drivers (first 2 years) and professional drivers: 0.3 g/l (0.15 mg/l breath)
answers.penalties: Over the limit: an administrative fine and points. Over 1.2 g/l or under the influence: 3–6 months in prison, a fine or community service, plus losing your licence for 1–4 years.

answers.headline: No. Where there’s a pedestrian crossing, you must use it, not cross nearby.
answers.summary: In areas with pedestrian crossings, pedestrians must cross the road at the crossing itself and not close to it. At crossings with lights, they must follow the pedestrian lights.

answers.headline: No. Killing someone is punished with 10 to 25 years in prison in Spain, and up to life in the worst cases.
answers.summary: Killing someone is homicide (homicidio). It becomes murder (asesinato) with treachery, for payment, with cruelty, or to commit or hide another crime. Some murders, for example of a child under 16 or a vulnerable person, carry reviewable life imprisonment. Self-defence can be lawful in narrow circumstances.
answers.penalties: Homicide: 10–15 years. Murder: 15–25 years. Aggravated murder: reviewable life imprisonment.

answers.headline: Everyone in Spain over 14 must have a DNI and show it when police ask.
answers.summary: The national identity card (DNI) is compulsory from age 14. Its holder must keep it valid, look after it, and show it when required by the authorities. Foreigners need their own valid identity document.

answers.headline: Not in public: using or carrying cannabis in public places is fined from €601.
answers.summary: Using or possessing illegal drugs, including cannabis, in public places, on the street, in public establishments or on public transport is a serious offence under the Public Safety Act, even if it isn’t for selling. Private use at home isn’t covered by this offence. Dealing is a crime under the Criminal Code.

answers.headline: No. Smoking is banned in all enclosed bars and restaurants in Spain.
answers.summary: Since 2011, smoking is banned in bars, restaurants and other enclosed food and drink establishments, as well as in workplaces, public buildings, and enclosed cinemas and theatres.
answers.regional_variation: The autonomous communities can add more smoke-free places.

answers.headline: No. Stealing is a crime in Spain: prison for items worth over €400, a fine below that.
answers.summary: Taking someone else’s movable property for gain, without the owner’s consent, is theft (hurto). Below €400 it’s usually punished with a fine, but repeat offenders with at least three earlier theft convictions get the prison penalty. Disabling alarms or security devices increases the penalty.
answers.penalties: Over €400: 6 to 18 months in prison. €400 or less: a fine of 1 to 3 months’ daily rates.

answers.headline: Yes, but only truly hands-free: without holding the phone and without earphones.
answers.summary: Using a mobile phone or other communication system while driving is banned, unless the communication happens without using your hands and without headphones or earphones. Screens with internet access or video are also banned while the vehicle moves.
answers.penalties: Using a phone in your hand: a traffic fine and points off your licence.

answers.headline: No. Radar detectors and jammers are banned in vehicles. Apps that show known camera locations are allowed.
answers.summary: It’s banned to install or carry radar jammers, radar detectors or any device meant to evade traffic enforcement. Warning systems that only show the position of speed cameras are excluded from the ban.
answers.penalties: A traffic fine and points off your licence.
answers.activity: Using a radar detector in a car
